title: In awe the wind blows
hookLine: in awe the wind blows and rivers run; only the Formless is without fear (Asa di Var, ang 464)

cards: Every morning the sun comes up within a few minutes of when the tables say it will. Tides arrive on schedule. Rivers that ran downhill in your grandparents' time still run downhill.

Nobody stands on the mountain telling the water where to go. Scientists call these patterns laws. Guru Nanak, looking at the same faithful river and punctual sun, reached for a word you might not expect.
Not law. Bhau. Fear, or awe.
And in one long salok he hears the entire universe living inside it.

teach.b: Bhau is the Punjabi word at the center of this salok on ang 464, and it's hard to put into English. It can mean fear.
But in Gurbani it often means something closer to reverence: the trembling respect of someone at the edge of a canyon. Listen to how the salok builds.
Bhai vich, in awe, the wind blows, always. In awe a hundred thousand rivers flow. In awe fire does its work.
In awe the earth carries its load. In awe Indra, lord of the rains, goes about head-down. In awe the sun and the moon travel their endless miles.
In awe stand the adepts and the gods, the warriors and the mighty heroes, and in awe the crowds of people come and go. Notice the pictures. Wind that never takes a day off.
Rivers that never refuse. Fire that keeps burning as if under orders. Guru Nanak is describing faithfulness.
Everything in creation keeps its place and does its job, because it moves within the One's hukam, the divine order. Bhau is what that looks like from the inside. Then the turn.
Awe, the salok says, is written on every forehead: sun, river, god, warrior.

teach.h: ONLY THE FORMLESS IS WITHOUT FEAR.
teach.b: Only one is without fear: the Formless, the One who is true. Tomorrow we stay with that line. For today, one thing.

In Sikh teaching, this awe isn't meant to make a person small and frightened. Elsewhere Gurbani pairs bhau with bhaau, awe with love, and some Sikh teachers describe the right kind of awe as what keeps love honest.
The wind doesn't blow out of terror. It blows because it knows where it belongs.

how: Sikhs hear this salok of awe in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and many know its refrain, bhai vich, in awe, from long listening in the gurdwara.

o: an order shouted by a king
fear, or awe, a trembling reverence

p: a hundred thousand flow in awe

s: in this salok, bhau only means being frightened
it can mean fear, but here it is closer to reverence, the awe of everything keeping its place.
the salok says awe is written on every forehead
sun, river, gods and warriors alike.
the salok leaves the gods and the warriors out of the list
adepts and gods, warriors and heroes all stand in awe too.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak, watching rivers that never stop running and a sun that never misses its rising. what word do you give it?
games.why: bhai vich: in awe the wind blows, the rivers flow, the sun and moon travel. only the Formless is without fear.

practice: Feel the air on your face, or your own breath, the small wind you carry everywhere, moving without being asked.
This air has moved faithfully since long before you and will move long after; let a little of the salok's awe settle in. If you pray, say Waheguru on the out-breath.

wordCard.voice: Bhau, awe or fear: Guru Nanak's picture of a faithful creation, wind, rivers, fire, earth, sun and moon, all moving bhai vich, in awe, within the One's order.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: in awe, in fear; the refrain that opens each line of the salok.

carryVoice: Your line: everything in awe. The wind knows where it belongs. Day five hundred forty-three, done.

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok M1 (bhai vich pavan vahai), Ang 464
